Cannabis Laws by State

Indiana Marijuana Laws: What Hoosiers Visiting Michigan Should Know

Short answer: no. As of October 2026, Indiana has no legal adult-use or medical marijuana. Here is what that means for Hoosiers who visit Michigan, and why nothing bought here can go back across the line.

Last reviewed October 2026

Indiana at a glance

  • Adult use: not legal in Indiana.

  • Medical: no medical marijuana program.

  • Possession: a crime for any amount; a first offense is a Class B misdemeanor, with up to 180 days in jail and a fine of up to $1,000.

  • In Michigan: adults 21 and older can shop with a valid ID and use cannabis on private property where the owner allows it.

  • Coming home: bringing Michigan cannabis into Indiana is illegal under Indiana law and federal law.

Is weed legal in Indiana?

No. As of October 2026, Indiana has no legal adult-use or medical marijuana, and possessing any amount is a crime. No bill changing that became law in 2026: the 2026 edition of the Indiana Code, published after that year’s session, keeps the possession law as it stood in 2025.

That sets Indiana apart from its neighbors. Michigan to the north and Illinois to the west both allow adults 21 and older to buy cannabis, and Ohio to the east legalized adult use in 2023. Hoosiers who visit Michigan can shop legally here, but the law changes the moment they cross back.

Possession penalties in Indiana

In Indiana, possessing marijuana is a Class B misdemeanor, punishable by up to 180 days in jail and a fine of up to $1,000. A prior drug conviction raises it to a Class A misdemeanor, with a jail term of up to one year and a fine of up to $5,000. With a prior drug conviction, 30 grams or more of marijuana, or 5 grams or more of hash oil or hashish, makes it a Level 6 felony.

Marijuana packaged to look like low-THC hemp extract also counts as a Class A misdemeanor when the person knew or should have known. Indiana law allows a one-time conditional discharge for a first misdemeanor possession offense.

None of these penalties depends on where the cannabis was bought.

Did federal rescheduling change anything?

Not for Indiana possession. A federal rule that took effect on April 28, 2026 moved only two things to Schedule III: FDA-approved drugs that contain marijuana, and marijuana covered by a state medical marijuana license. All other marijuana, adult-use included, is still in Schedule I as of October 2026. A broader proposal to move all marijuana to Schedule III went to a federal hearing in the summer of 2026; as of late October the judge’s recommended decision was still pending and no final rule had been published.

None of that touches Indiana’s own law, which still makes possession a crime. And the April rule is aimed at licensed medical businesses: it does not say that patients may carry medical marijuana across state lines.

Hemp, THCA and the federal changes

Federal law has been narrowing what counts as legal hemp. Congress set a new definition that counts THCA toward hemp’s 0.3% THC limit and excludes finished products with more than 0.4 mg of total THC per container. Most intoxicating hemp-THC products stop qualifying as hemp. The change was set for November 12, 2026, and a stopgap law pushed most of it to December 11, 2026.

On the Michigan side, cannabis over 0.3% THC, THCA included, is marijuana that only licensed marijuana businesses may sell, and delta-8 THC counts as marijuana too. Read the label of anything you buy, and buy cannabis only from a licensed store.

Hoosiers shopping in Michigan

Michigan’s adult-use law covers adults 21 and older, and you do not need a Michigan ID to buy. Every Michigan store checks a valid driver’s license or government-issued photo ID before a sale, and our New Buffalo pages note that, in most cases, valid government IDs from other states are accepted. Bring your ID to confirm.

While you are here, Michigan’s limits apply to you: up to 2.5 ounces per transaction and in your possession, with no more than 15 grams of it as concentrate. Use cannabis only on private property where the owner allows it. Public use is not allowed, hotels and other property owners may ban it, and no one may use cannabis while driving or smoke it in a vehicle on a public road.

Michigan has no numeric THC limit for drivers, but it bans driving under the influence and has a zero-tolerance law for any amount of a Schedule 1 drug, which includes marijuana. If you have used cannabis, do not drive.

Nothing bought in Michigan goes back to Indiana

Bringing Michigan-bought cannabis into Indiana is illegal under Indiana law, regardless of where it was bought, and taking cannabis across any state line is illegal under federal law. That includes products you did not finish, so buy only what you will enjoy in Michigan.

Friendly reminder: Enjoy responsibly in Michigan—don’t travel across state lines with cannabis.

Indiana visitor questions

Is weed legal in Indiana?

No. As of October 2026, Indiana has no legal adult-use or medical marijuana, and possessing any amount is a crime.

Can Indiana residents buy cannabis in Michigan?

Yes. Adults 21 and older can buy here with a valid driver’s license or other government photo ID, and Michigan’s limits and rules apply while you are in the state.

Can I bring weed from Michigan to Indiana?

No. It is illegal under Indiana law, wherever it was bought, and crossing a state line with cannabis is illegal under federal law.

What is the penalty for possession in Indiana?

A first offense is a Class B misdemeanor, with up to 180 days in jail and a fine of up to $1,000. A prior drug conviction makes it a Class A misdemeanor.

Does Indiana have a medical marijuana program?

No. Indiana has no legal medical marijuana, and a Michigan medical card is only for Michigan residents.

Where can I use cannabis I buy in Michigan?

On private property in Michigan where the owner allows it. Public use is not allowed, and no one may use cannabis while driving.

Did federal rescheduling make cannabis legal in Indiana?

No. The April 2026 federal rule moved only FDA-approved marijuana drugs and state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III, and Indiana’s own law still makes possession a crime.

This guide is general information about Indiana and Michigan law as of October 2026, not legal advice. Laws change; check the official sources above before you rely on a detail.
